cultivar: Lingyun Baihao (downy large-leaf) and Guangxi medium- and large-leaf population bushes; Yunnan large-leaf in newer gardens
processing: Fully oxidised: withered, rolled, oxidised in Guangxi's warm humid conditions and dried; the downy Lingyun Baihao buds keep thick golden fur through oxidation.
harvest_season: Spring (March–April) is the best; the subtropical climate allows summer and autumn pickings, which are cheaper and heavier.
appearance_dry: Fat, twisted dark strands with abundant golden, fuzzy tips; bud-only lots look almost entirely gold.
appearance_liquor: Bright red-orange with a golden ring.
appearance_wet: Large, soft copper-red leaves with golden buds.
taste_profile: Honey and sweet potato with malt and a caramel sweetness, soft tannin and a smooth, simple finish.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at around 90 °C, short steeps; bud-heavy lots like it a touch cooler. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, with summer and autumn lots following; drink within a year. Guangxi bud tea is said in the trade to be sold under other names too, so a label that says Gui Hong or Guangxi is the plain version. Not aged.
description:
Gui Hong is the black tea of Guangxi, the subtropical region south-west of Guangdong, and it has a split identity. Under its own name it is a modest regional gongfu black, reportedly made since the 1960s, best known from Lingyun in the Baise hills and from Zhaoping in the east; under other people's names, the trade often says, it is a source of 'golden bud' black tea, sold as Jin Jun Mei or as Yunnan gold by traders who would rather not say Guangxi on the box. That second part is widely repeated and not documented.

The reason is the plant. Lingyun Baihao, 'Lingyun white down', is a large-leaf local cultivar with buds covered in thick white fur that turns a deep gold when oxidised, and Guangxi's warm, humid climate makes a fast, even black-tea oxidation easy. The leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried in the standard way, and what comes out is pretty, tippy and sweet.

In the cup it is honey, sweet potato and caramel over soft malt with a gentle tannin and a smooth, uncomplicated finish; six or seven steeps at around 90 °C, or an easy three-minute pot. It is a pleasant, friendly black tea whose only fault is a lack of the length and complexity that Tongmu or old-tree Yunnan bring – which matters only when it has been sold as those.

It is sold as the current spring, mostly within Guangxi and Guangdong, with bud-heavy lots at the top; at its real price it is good value among tippy blacks. Look for fat, downy golden tips and a sweet, malty dry aroma. If a 'Jin Jun Mei' is uniformly gold, fluffy and cheap, it is unlikely to be from Tongmu and it may well come from Guangxi or another big-leaf region, and it is worth knowing that so you can buy such tea as itself next time.

Try it alongside a Yunnan Golden Buds: same big-leaf sweetness, two provinces, and a useful lesson in what region adds.
sources_note: The claim that much Guangxi bud tea is sold as Jin Jun Mei or Yunnan tea is widely reported in the Chinese tea trade but not officially documented. Lingyun Baihao is a registered national cultivar; 1960s start of Gui Hong gongfu production follows Chinese sources.
history:
Very little is documented about Gui Hong under this name. Guangxi black tea plainly exists, but what is written about the region's tea is mostly about Liu Bao, jasmine and green teas. Tao of Tea's map of Guangxi lists Lingyun Baimao, which appears to be the same downy local tea as Lingyun Baihao, among the region's famous teas, without mentioning a black version.

The start of production in the 1960s and the talk of Guangxi buds being sold under other names are trade accounts with no documented source. Take this as a modest regional black whose story still has to be written.
